candidateRows: Human behavior is sufficiently determined by prior causes that an appeal to freely choosing among genuine alternatives is unnecessary.
This states the con side's governing thesis and causal model, directly denying the kind of alternative-controlling freedom described by the motion.
At the start of his opening statement, Sapolsky defines determinism through an uninterrupted regress of prior causes and applies it to human conduct.
Behavioral choices reflect causal influences operating across moments, physiology, development, genes, culture, and deep history.
The multi-timescale causal survey supplies the principal empirical support for the claim that choices attributed to free will arise from antecedent conditions.
Sapolsky moves backward from immediate environmental cues through hormones, trauma, childhood, fetal development, genetics, culture, and ancestral history.
Biological and environmental explanations form one integrated causal account rather than leaving an explanatory gap for free will.
The synthesis converts a collection of influences into the stronger exclusionary conclusion required by the con position on genuinely available alternatives.
After warning against single-factor explanations, Sapolsky argues that genetic, neural, developmental, cultural, and environmental accounts are causally continuous.
Free will consists in having multiple possibilities available with control over which possibility becomes actual.
This defines the pro position and connects alternative possibilities to responsibility, normative judgment, and the reactive attitudes named in the motion.
Huemer contrasts libertarian freedom with hard determinism, then argues that judgments of obligation and responsibility presuppose genuine alternatives.
Ordinary practices of deliberation, advice, evaluation, reward, and retributive punishment become inappropriate if no alternatives ever exist.
It argues that denying alternative possibilities conflicts with pervasive responsibility-related and reason-guided practices, supporting the claim that freedom matters.
Huemer surveys practical activities that distinguish possible courses of action and contends that each loses its point when every act is unavoidable or impossible.
Accepting, arguing for, or rationally believing determinism is self-defeating because those activities presuppose alternatives and normative reasons.
This is Huemer's principal epistemic objection: deterministic advocacy allegedly relies on deliberation, reasons, and rational norms that determinism itself cannot sustain.
Huemer develops linked problems concerning deliberation, argumentation, and rational norms, concluding that a coherent rational endorsement of determinism is unavailable.
The felt obviousness of free choice is unreliable because intuitively compelling explanations have repeatedly yielded to mechanistic accounts.
This directly challenges the epistemic basis of Huemer's appeal to what deliberation and responsibility seem to presuppose, weakening a central pro argument.
Huemer's claim that free will is supported by intuitive judgments about alternatives, responsibility, and rational practice.
Sapolsky compares free-will intuitions with historically mistaken intuitive explanations and with experiments revealing unnoticed influences on stated preferences.
The absence of free will is compatible with behavioral change because changing conditions mechanistically alter organisms and their later responses.
The move answers the practical objection that determinism makes deliberation or intervention pointless by distinguishing causal change from freely choosing to change.
Huemer's contention that deliberation, advice, and other change-directed practices make no sense if determinism is true.
Sapolsky rejects the idea that predetermination entails stasis and describes learning and altered threat responses as mechanistic forms of change.
Evidence that outside factors influence some decisions does not establish complete determination or eliminate freedom in unimpaired cases.
This directly attacks the inference from causal influence to exhaustive determination and disputes generalizing from impaired decisions to ordinary reason-responsive agency.
Sapolsky's multi-timescale examples offered to show that antecedent biological and environmental influences leave no room for free will.
Huemer separates influence from determination and argues that examples involving hunger, trauma, or disorder do not address well-functioning, reason-guided decisions.
Intellectual appearances remain indispensable to justification, and attacks on free will themselves depend on intuitive and logical appearances.
The move defends the evidential method underlying Huemer's case and argues that rejecting intuition wholesale would also undermine the con side's reasoning and logic.
Sapolsky's argument that historically false intuitions and unnoticed causal influences make intuition an unreliable guide to free will.
Huemer narrows the philosophical meaning of intuition, grounds justification in appearances, and argues that causal and responsibility judgments also rely on intuitions.
Determinism permits change only when that change is itself determined, leaving people unable to control what happens.
The move directly connects determinism to the absence of control, addressing the motion's central contrast between determined outcomes and genuinely available actions.
The earlier claim that determinism remains compatible with meaningful change and efforts to alter future outcomes.
After defending intuitions as unavoidable foundations of belief, Huemer answers the contention that determinism is compatible with change by distinguishing change from control over change.
Even if abandoning free will makes social life difficult to envision, retributive punishment and differential moral entitlement still do not make sense.
The move directly addresses whether freedom justifies responsibility, denying the legitimacy of retribution and earned moral standing despite uncertainty about replacement practices.
Huemer's warning that determinism is hopeless and that denying freedom threatens responsibility, blame, punishment, and ordinary social functioning.

Sapolsky acknowledges disciplinary differences and concedes that a society without free-will-based praise or blame is hard to imagine, but argues that practical uncertainty cannot change how agency actually works.
A purely deterrent and incapacitative account of punishment cannot explain why framing an innocent ex-convict is wrong while punishing the actual offender is permissible.
The example is a central defense of desert-based responsibility, arguing that consequentialist rationales cannot preserve the morally crucial distinction between guilty and innocent targets.
Sapolsky's contention that retribution never makes sense and that punishment should not express differential moral entitlement.

Huemer first notes that determinists can retain deterrent punishment while rejecting retribution, then tests that position with a case where framing an innocent former offender would seemingly achieve the same deterrence and incapacitation.
Scientific understanding has repeatedly made society more humane by replacing blame and retribution with causal explanations of behavior.
The historical argument supports the denial that responsibility-based retribution is necessary and links causal explanation directly to reduced punishment and increased humane treatment.
Huemer's claim that the wrongness of secretly framing an innocent person demonstrates the necessity of a retributive rationale.

Sapolsky contrasts older punitive interpretations of contamination, seizures, schizophrenia, and learning difficulties with later causal explanations that removed blame without producing social collapse.
Past error does not generally undermine present belief; rational action must use current best judgments unless past mistakes specifically bear on those judgments.
The move challenges the main inductive basis offered for extending causal exculpation to all conduct and defends reliance on current judgments about responsibility.
Sapolsky's historical induction that future people will regard current practices of praise, blame, and retribution as cruel errors.

After Sapolsky predicts that future knowledge will expose current responsibility judgments as mistaken, Huemer argues that mere similarity to confidently held past errors is too broad to defeat every present belief.
Because no neural action can be shown independent of biological and environmental causes, expanding causal knowledge warrants deep caution about blame and deserved advantage.

This is a direct empirical and moral challenge to libertarian agency: proof of an action independent of antecedent influences would establish freedom, but current evidence instead supports caution about responsibility.
Huemer's argument that historical mistakes do not undermine present responsibility beliefs without a specific evidential connection.

Sapolsky reframes uncertainty asymmetrically, demanding an example of a neuron acting independently of hormones, genes, development, and environment, while emphasizing the rapid growth of causal knowledge and harms caused by mistaken responsibility attributions.
Absent decisive scientific evidence either way, the rational default is to accept the appearance that one has free will.
The move supplies the affirmative side's burden-of-proof framework, treating experienced freedom as presumptively real until sufficiently strong contrary evidence is produced.
Sapolsky's neuron challenge and appeal to the accelerating accumulation of biological and environmental explanations of behavior.

Huemer allows that a perfect predictive brain model could strongly support determinism and predictive failure could support freedom, but maintains that neither has been established and appearances therefore set the default.
Mechanistic intervention and scientific discovery repeatedly expose intuitions as unreliable, while existing evidence already shows substantially less freedom in morally important domains.

The move attacks the affirmative epistemic default and argues that demonstrated causal influence is already extensive enough to require revising responsibility judgments even without complete proof of determinism.
Huemer's claims that appearances should be trusted by default and that both moral progress and scientific reasoning ultimately depend on intuition.

Sapolsky argues that drugs, social interventions, laboratory science, and counterintuitive discoveries can distinguish reliable appearances from error, then urges revision of present values as causal knowledge grows.
Influences can alter the probability and felt difficulty of a choice without wholly determining it, leaving at least some easy decisions free.
The answer directly defends the motion's requirement of genuinely available alternatives by explaining how causal influence could coexist with undetermined choice.
The audience challenge asking what partial determination means and how unconscious influences can coexist with a genuinely free choice.
Huemer admits he lacks a deeper mechanism, but proposes that outside factors make one option more likely and make choosing feel easier or harder rather than eliminating alternative possibilities.
Science does not presuppose determinism, because indeterministic theories are scientific and reasons can explain behavior without determining it.
The move rejects the proposed link between scientific explanation and determinism, preserving the conceptual possibility that free choices remain scientifically intelligible.
The audience suggestion that scientific practice presupposes determinism because science seeks explanations for why choices occur.

In response to a question about whether free choices must be brute facts, Huemer separates explanation from deterministic causation and points to both indeterministic science and explanations citing an agent's reasons.
A free choice can be explained by the agent's reasons even though the final selection among competing reasons may have no further explanation.
The claim directly addresses whether libertarian choice must be wholly inexplicable and identifies the precise point at which explanation terminates.
The audience challenge that a genuinely free choice may be an unexplained brute fact.
After both speakers distinguish scientific explanation from prediction, Huemer returns to the second part of the question concerning explanations of free decisions.
Behavior never reaches an unexplained act of selection because every decision remains attributable to prior causes, while quantum indeterminacy cannot supply agency.
This states the hard-determinist alternative to libertarian choice and blocks quantum indeterminacy as a proposed route to genuine agency.
Huemer's claim that explanation can end with the agent simply deciding among competing reasons.
Sapolsky immediately contrasts Huemer's stopping point with an indefinitely prior-causal account and then addresses a familiar quantum-indeterminacy objection.
Gratitude can be explained through its evolutionary support for reciprocity and through proximal neural mechanisms without requiring freely chosen helping.
The account supports determinism's ability to explain morally significant emotions that might otherwise seem to presuppose freely chosen conduct.
The audience suggestion that gratitude lacks an evolutionary rationale if helpers have no choice.
An audience question asks why gratitude evolved if beneficiaries recognize that helpful conduct was not freely chosen; Sapolsky answers at several explanatory levels.
Known biological and environmental causes of behavior rule out every philosophically significant conception of free will, including compatibilist versions.
This is Sapolsky's direct thesis on the motion and connects denial of free will to revising practices of blame, reward, and punishment.
The compatibilist alternative proposed by the audience as a less radical response to causal determination.
Asked why he is not merely a compatibilist, Sapolsky says contemporary knowledge leaves no room for free will and draws responsibility-related implications.
If determinism were established, ordinary paradigm cases would warrant revising the concept of free will toward compatibilism rather than eliminating freedom altogether.
The argument explains why Huemer rejects hard determinism as the proper conceptual consequence even under a hypothetical acceptance of determinism.
Sapolsky's contention that determination excludes every meaningful conception of free will, including compatibilist accounts.
Following Sapolsky's hard-incompatibilist answer, Huemer explains how concepts should preserve their ordinary paradigm applications and applies that method to freedom.
Determinism entails that acting otherwise would require a different past, so no one could do otherwise, which conflicts with the ordinary conception of free will.
This supplies Huemer's central incompatibilist argument linking a fixed past under determinism to the absence of genuinely available alternative actions.
Huemer moves from his conceptual methodology to a student-grade example, derives a principle about past conditions, and applies it to deterministic action.
People can exercise control over beliefs when evidence is nonconclusive, and weighing epistemic reasons is a deliberative choice process analogous to choosing actions.
The move protects the pro case's appeal to rational deliberation by arguing that constrained belief formation does not eliminate meaningful control.
The doxastic-involuntarist objection that people do not choose beliefs and therefore do not choose determinism or free will.
An audience member challenges Huemer's deliberation argument by asking whether beliefs are chosen; Huemer distinguishes evidential constraint from absence of control.
The normative term should cannot merely mean that an outcome would be better, because that interpretation recommends actions beyond an agent's capabilities and defeats practical advice.
The semantic argument defends the pro side's claim that genuine normative requirements presuppose feasible alternatives rather than mere outcome rankings.
The proposed deterministic account on which should only means that an outcome would be better, without implying alternative possibilities.
The final audience question offers alternative deterministic meanings for normative and epistemic language; Huemer first answers the proposal about practical obligation.
A purely microphysical determinism threatens reasoning because electrical and chemical processes are not themselves responsive to truth or to the quality of epistemic reasons.
The claim preserves a major anti-determinist argument by explaining why causal production by microphysical events may not amount to rational responsiveness.
The objection that deterministic causes could track good epistemic reasons and make beliefs follow the evidence without choice.
After the moderator restates the epistemic part of the final question, Huemer interprets the earlier Lucas argument as targeting microphysical causal determination.
